You recently published a letter stating that several Southern States had, by statutes, integrated bars, the only qualification for membership being a license to practice law, such associations being strictly professional.

The difference between the District of Columbia Bar Association and the other associations is that the local bar association is also a social organization, its charter reading as follows:

The District of Columbia Bar Association is a corporation, organized under the laws of the District of Columbia, by private individuals. It is not a public corporation and has no official connection with the courts of the District, and membership in it is restricted by its bylaws to such persons as may be elected to membership therein by its board of directors, the qualifications for membership being set forth in bylaws adopted by the corporation pursuant to authority of law. There are several other bar associations in the District of Columbia, organized and chartered under the same District law, which have likewise restricted membership therein; namely:

1. Washington Bar Association, for colored attorneys.

2. Federal Bar Association, for Government attorneys.

3. Patent Bar Association, for patent attorneys.

4. Women's Bar Association, for women attorneys.

These associations were organized to serve the interests of particular groups, and the legality and propriety of such associations have not been questioned.

People of any race, religion or political faith may assemble and associate for the advancement of their interests. No sound public policy would destroy the interesting diversity of life. If the aim and end of democracy should be to reduce all men to the same shape and shade and common opinion, then it could and should not survive. It would counter one of the fundamental principles of evolution.

There is no single organization of attorneys in the District which represents all the special interest groups. It would be a simple matter to organize a central council of bar associations composed of delegates from all the groups, and the writer has suggested such an organization as the solution to the local situation, but it would appear that a certain group operating in the District is not interested in a solution but only in the destruction of the Bar Association of the District of Columbia as an all-white group.

St. Paul -- Municipal Judge Leonard J. Keyes dismissed charges of gambling against the persons arrested in a raid early Saturday, July 10, at 40 Kent in St. Paul.


The 20 scheduled for trial Saturday, July 20, were freed on the basis of a motion submitted by Jack Wallace, defense counsel, who pointed out the fact that no evidence of individual gambling had been presented in the charges and that the law under which the men were charged specifically states that one must visit and bet in a gambling house to be guilty of a gambling charge.


Judge Keyes concurred with Wallace's motion saying that while he felt that the evidence did point to the fact that the house was being used as a gambling place there was indeed no evidence of individual gambling.


Detectives and police officers who entered the house in the early morning raid testified that they saw a group of men scrambling to pick up money from the large table but did not see anyone in the actual act of gambling.


Several decks of cards and numerous loose cards together with four sets of dice—including an obviously crooked pair—were introduced as evidence.


Police intend keeping a close watch on the house to prevent its future use for gambling. Many reports indicate, however, that the place will be boycotted by former habituees because of the crooked equipment turned up in the raid by police.


One of the defendants, Marion Dooley of 500 Charles, was forced to forfeit $25 bail because he did not appear until court proceedings were finished. According to Dooley's statement to the court, "An oversight, your honor." The charge of gambling was dropped as in the case of the other 20 defendants.
